experiment: Trip 9: a capture's inner loop (read a chunk, write it to the card, CRC32 it) measured three ways on the real drive and card: sequential PIO, sequential DMA, and DMA double-buffered so the drive fills the next chunk while the CPU writes and hashes this one. 4096 sectors at FAD 45150, two runs. No dump written.

hardware.note: Image+BSS 2545892 -> 2697092 (+151 KB), the two 32-sector pipeline buffers, as designed.

correctness.meaning: All three paths CRC32 the same 9,633,792 bytes. One value across six rows means the overlapped path returned exactly the bytes the sequential paths did.

projection.method: T7's disc time scaled by the fraction of read time the overlap left behind, the rest unchanged. A projection, not a capture.

conclusions: The overlap works on hardware: 92.4% of the DMA read time disappears behind the SD write (2020 ms to 153 ms), and the overlapped run lands 1.9% above the floor of write+CRC32 alone. There is almost nothing left to recover on the read side.
Rate: 752.9 KiB/s sequential PIO, 846.3 sequential DMA, 1009.8 overlapped: 34.1% over what the engine does today.
The bytes are identical: one CRC32 (66f88083) across all six rows.
The CPU census shows where the gain comes from: sequential DMA leaves the worker idle 2024 ms while the drive works; overlapped leaves only 260 ms, having spent the rest writing.
Sequential DMA alone is already 12.4% faster than PIO, because a DMA read of buffered data costs less wall time than pulling the same bytes through the CPU.
Projected onto the real T7 capture: 26.7 minutes becomes about 19.8, or about 17.7 with the measured CRC16 and CRC32 replacements as well.

limitations: The pipeline is not the capture engine: it has no EDC check, no checkpoints, no SHA-256, no retry path and no resume. The engine still reads with PIO and is unchanged.
One drive, one disc, one card, two runs, inner radius only.
A real overlapped engine cannot overlap the first read or the last write, and must keep checkpointing, cancellation and retries correct at every interleaving.
